accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters (3 and 4 year olds: use all their senses in hands-on exploration of natural materials; explore collections of materials with similar and different properties; talk about the differences between materials) and the National Curriculum Year 1 Everyday materials statements (describe the simple physical properties of everyday materials; compare and group materials on the basis of their simple physical properties). Every sort is right: teddy and bread soft, stone and spoon hard; pineapple skin and bark rough, apple and spoon smooth; balloon and sock stretchy, pencil and stone not; ball hard and smooth, brick hard and rough, silk ribbon soft and smooth; wool for a soft bed, bricks for a hard wall, paper towel absorbent.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-materials confusions: soft and smooth used as synonyms (prediction 'A ball is smooth. Is it soft too?' and feedback 'Smooth is not soft'), hard assumed to mean rough (prediction 'Is every hard thing rough?' disproved by the smooth spoon), judging by looks or colour instead of a touch test (challenge 'A red rock'), and guessing without testing (sorting before pressing says 'Press the teddy first. Does it squash?').

lab_distinct.evidence: Each property has its own touch test on the canvas: pressing squashes soft things with a dent while hard ones only jolt, dragging across draws a zigzag trail for rough and a straight glide for smooth, dragging sideways stretches stretchy things that spring back on an elastic ease, and a two-row word picker gives one thing two properties. No other flagship lab simulates touch tests; the 30% shingle gate passed against all of them, including flagfeel, flagheavy and flagsize.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child presses, strokes or pulls before sorting, and the canvas shows what happened (It squashes! / It slides along. / It stretches, then springs back!), so the word comes from the test. The two-words step makes them separate the press test from the stroke test, and the jobs step applies properties to a purpose, matching the evidence 'picks a soft material for a teddy's bed and says why'.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Yes, hard means rough' (the next sort shows a hard spoon that slides) and 'Yes, smooth means soft' for a ball (the press test in the two-words step shows it does not squash, and choosing Soft is refused with 'Smooth is not soft').

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve tagged messages: a squashing sponge called hard or rough, a spoon called rough or soft, a brick or a coloured rock as a teddy bed, bumpy bark called smooth or soft, a marble called soft or rough, and a stretched balloon that stays long or breaks. Each message names the test that settles it.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are short sentences about a teddy, a stone, bark and a spoon and pass the family limit; canvas text is two to five words with big emoji and two big sorting bins. Adult text stays under grade 10 and uses the exact terms material, property, physical properties, hard, soft, rough, smooth, stretchy and absorbent.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler patterns and the 12% duplicate gate against every lesson, including Grouping materials and the states-of-matter lessons. Each kid paragraph adds one test or idea; adult paragraphs cover curriculum goals, which test gives which word, common mistakes and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots of all six steps mid-task: the object card, the two sorting bins, the four word tiles and the three job cards fit at 360 px with readable labels; the count label was moved clear of the card after the first screenshot pass; young-class buttons sit under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in light and dark themes, no console errors. Every gesture has a button (Press, Stroke, Pull, each bin, each word, Check, each job choice) and the canvas aria-label announces what the finger felt and each sort result.
